children.title: Trump DOJ Orders Review of FBI Personnel Tied to January 6 Cases Before Patel Takes Office
children.description_short: On Jan. 31, 2025, DOJ ordered a review of personnel tied to Jan. 6 cases, before Kash Patel became FBI director.
children.description_medium: On January 31, 2025, Reuters reported that acting Deputy Attorney General Emil Bove directed federal prosecutors to list employees who worked on the January 6 Capitol investigation, while FBI officials tied to those cases faced personnel actions. The report described Patel as the nominee to lead the FBI, not its director. It does not substantiate a claim that Patel fired hundreds of agents for disloyalty.
children.description_long: On January 31, 2025, the Trump administration began a round of Justice Department and FBI personnel actions focused in part on staff who had worked on investigations related to the January 6 attack. Reuters reported that acting Deputy Attorney General Emil Bove told federal prosecutors to compile a list of prosecutors and FBI agents who participated in the Capitol investigation. The same report said a memo ordered eight FBI officials to resign or face dismissal because of their work on January 6 cases, and separately described about 20 probationary prosecutors fired under a Bove order. Reuters also reported that the FBI Agents Association warned potentially hundreds of agents could be affected; that was a warning about possible scale, not a reported count of agents already fired. Kash Patel was still the nominee to direct the bureau and had appeared at a confirmation hearing the day before. This episode therefore belongs to Trump administration and Justice Department actions before Patel became FBI director. The reporting supports a personnel review and identified removals, but does not establish that Patel fired hundreds of agents for insufficient loyalty.

children.title: FBI Forces Out at Least Three Senior Officials, Including Brian Driscoll
children.description_short: The FBI forced out at least three senior officials in August 2025, including former acting director Brian Driscoll.
children.description_medium: The Washington Post reported that the FBI forced out at least three senior officials during a period of conflict with the Trump administration. One was former acting director Brian Driscoll, who had resisted demands to identify agents involved in January 6 investigations. The report places these departures during Kash Patel’s tenure, but does not say every official was dismissed for the same reason.
children.description_long: On August 7, 2025, The Washington Post reported that the FBI had forced out at least three senior officials who had clashed with the Trump administration. One was Brian Driscoll, the bureau’s former acting director during the first weeks of Trump’s second term. The report said Driscoll was fired by senior leaders and would finish his last day on Friday, August 8; the people quoted said he was given no reason for the firing. During his brief time leading the bureau, Driscoll had resisted demands from Trump Justice Department appointees to identify agents who worked on January 6 investigations. The article said he later provided the department a list of more than 5,000 FBI personnel identified only by employee identification number. It placed the departures during Kash Patel’s tenure. This is a distinct August personnel episode from the January 2025 review and the February 2026 agent dismissals. The source does not establish that all three officials worked on January 6 cases, that the same decisionmaker fired each one, or that a formal written rationale was issued. It documents reported departures amid a wider dispute over the treatment of bureau personnel.

children.title: FBI Fires at Least a Dozen Agents Tied to Trump Classified-Documents Probe
children.description_short: The FBI fired at least a dozen staff tied to Trump’s classified-documents probe in February 2026, The Washington Post reported.
children.description_medium: On February 26, 2026, The Washington Post reported that FBI Director Kash Patel had fired at least a dozen agents and staff across the country who were tied to the probe into Donald Trump’s alleged mishandling of classified documents after he left office in 2021. This is a separate Patel-era episode; the report does not support the original claim that hundreds were fired for insufficient loyalty.
children.description_long: On February 26, 2026, The Washington Post reported that FBI Director Kash Patel had fired at least a dozen agents and staff across the country during that week. The article connected those employees to the FBI probe into Donald Trump’s alleged mishandling of classified documents after leaving office in 2021. It described the dismissals as a continuation of Patel’s purge of bureau employees. This is a separate, later episode from the January 2025 review directed by acting Deputy Attorney General Emil Bove and the August 2025 departures of senior FBI officials. The available report supports the number “at least a dozen” for this specific week and describes the employees as tied to the classified-documents investigation. It does not establish that hundreds of agents were dismissed, that every affected employee was deemed insufficiently loyal, or that the February 2026 dismissals included employees tied to the separate 2020-election investigation. The original combined entry blended these episodes and attributed the January review to Patel before he led the bureau. This card preserves the Washington Post’s reported connection and allegation wording without turning the report into an independent finding about each employee or the president.

children.title: Knowles Fire Burnover Kills Four Firefighters
children.description_short: A June 27 burnover at the Knowles Fire killed three firefighters at the scene; a fourth died July 24 from injuries sustained in the same incident.
children.description_medium: A burnover during firefighting operations at Montana’s Knowles Fire on June 27, 2025, killed three firefighters at the scene. A fourth firefighter, Nathan Matthews, died on July 24 from injuries sustained in that same burnover. The two dates describe one incident and its later fatality, not separate events.
children.description_long: On June 27, 2025, a burnover occurred during firefighting operations at Montana’s Knowles Fire. Three firefighters died at the scene. Nathan Matthews, who was critically injured in the same incident, died on July 24, 2025. The later date marks his death from injuries sustained in the June 27 burnover; it does not describe a second fire or a separate fatal event. The two original child cards therefore cover one discrete incident and should be consolidated to avoid counting the same burnover twice. The combined record should state the four deaths and preserve the documented sequence: the burnover, three deaths at the scene, and Matthews’s later death. The supplied sources describe this as an operational fire-line accident; they do not establish that a Trump administration policy caused the burnover. The card should remain within scope only if the collection includes significant public-safety events without a demonstrated administration link. This draft does not infer such a link.

children.title: Interior Orders Review to Unleash American Energy
children.description_short: Interior directed agencies to review rules and practices that could constrain domestic energy production.
children.description_medium: On February 3, 2025, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum announced six new Secretary’s Orders, including Order 3418. The Department said it would encourage energy production on federal lands and review agency actions that could burden domestic energy development. The documented action is a policy direction; the sources do not establish resulting drilling or environmental effects.
children.description_long: On February 3, 2025, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum announced that he had signed six Secretary’s Orders on his first day in office. The Department described Secretary’s Order 3418, “Unleashing American Energy,” as aligning Interior with the president’s energy policy, encouraging energy exploration and production on federal lands and waters, and requiring review of agency actions that could burden domestic energy-resource development. The order also directed review of certain appropriations. This card records the policy direction and review instructions, not a measured change in drilling, leasing outcomes, or environmental conditions. The original entry’s Wyoming acreage and migration-corridor claims concern later lease events and are separated into another child. No 28-day permitting guarantee, acreage figure, or migration-corridor effect is carried into this copy because the accessed evidence for the February order does not establish those claims. The record identifies a federal policy direction with nationwide reach across Interior; operational effects and environmental outcomes remain unknown.

children.title: BLM Leases 114,439 Acres in June 2026 Wyoming Oil and Gas Sale
children.description_short: BLM offered 114,439 acres in Wyoming leases; the packet reports a sale, not drilling or production.
children.description_medium: On June 9, 2026, BLM reported leasing 102 Wyoming parcels totaling about 114,439 acres for $34.7 million in receipts. Its earlier notice had proposed 108 parcels and 119,595 acres. The sources establish a completed lease sale, not actual drilling or wildlife effects; leasing is only the first step before separate permit review.
children.description_long: On June 9, 2026, the Bureau of Land Management reported that it leased 102 Wyoming parcels totaling approximately 114,439 acres in a quarterly oil and gas sale, with $34,706,638 in total receipts. In March, the agency had announced 108 parcels totaling 119,595 acres for a planned June sale, so the final sale did not match the earlier offered-parcel total in the held entry. BLM states that leasing is the first step in federal oil and gas development and that an operator must submit an application for a permit to drill before development can begin. The supplied claim that the sale covered 250,000 acres near Yellowstone and Grand Teton or overlapped named wildlife migration corridors is not supported by the accessed sale notices and is omitted. These sources document leases and receipts, not actual drilling, production, emissions, or specific wildlife effects. The receipt total is reported by BLM and is not treated here as long-term government revenue or private profit. The event is a completed lease sale; later development and environmental outcomes remain unknown.

source_fact_map.fact: BLM announced a planned June 2026 sale of 108 parcels totaling 119,595 Wyoming acres.
source_fact_map.quote: to offer 108 oil and gas parcels totaling 119,595 acres in Wyoming.
source_fact_map.source_excerpt: The Bureau of Land Management today announced an oil and gas lease sale scheduled for June 2, 2026, to offer 108 oil and gas parcels totaling 119,595 acres in Wyoming. The BLM completed scoping on these parcels in November 2025 and held a public comment period that closed in January 2026 on the parcels and the related environmental analysis. A 30-day public protest period to receive additional public input opened today and will close April 20, 2026. Leasing is the first step in the process to develop federal oil and gas resources. Before development operations can begin, an operator must submit an application for permit to drill detailing development plans.
